analysis.title: GS Basics - Liquidation. 1998 or 2000. VVIX.
key_insights: Sharp US liquidation on 6 Nov 2026 report date: Nasdaq -5.5%, SOX -12%, SPX -4.4%. Day one post election saw AI underperform while the broader market rallied on a perceived pivot to the political center, led by quality, cyclicals and short covering. Day two was a catch down.
The author argues that if data center construction slows sharply, nominal growth expectations look unrealistic, leaving the cyclicals that rallied Wednesday mispriced.
Leveraged ETF rebalancing likely added to the decline in semis and NDX with mechanical selling into the close. Combined with negative dealer gamma, the author calls it a self-reinforcing liquidation.
VVIX had its largest one-day move since Feb 5, 2018.

Energy reversed higher as fears of escalation added to market worries. Oil rebounded roughly 4% the prior day and was higher again in the morning. Markets got ahead of themselves pricing an immediate Iran off ramp, and negotiations remain unresolved.
Cash franchise net sold -$3bn, with Tech (Info Tech + Comm Services) -$2.2bn of that. The Tech unwind extends to -$27bn since it began, larger than the July technical unwind's -$21bn.
GS AIS flags semis pressure. The real problem is the absence of underlying demand, particularly from long-only funds. Multi-strat, quant, long-only and retail are all moving in the same direction.

The author's 1998 vs 2000 framing: speed and size of moves point to acute leverage and forced de-grossing. Correlations are rising, momentum is underperforming, the residual leverage factor is selling off and low beta, safety and quality are bid. The author leans toward 1998, a liquidity event with intact growth.

Supporting the 1998 read: today's AI leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets. Delaying data centers does not destroy compute demand, and constrained capacity may improve existing economics. The uncomfortable parallel with 2000 is the scale of spending and uncertainty about returns.

Four AI concerns drive the selloff: insufficient capital to finance the buildout, insufficient revenue to justify investment, insufficient power and permitting capacity, and an unsustainable aggregate spending path. The author says the market has latched onto power and permitting, arguably the least important. The real question is whether revenues justify the capital employed.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's rhetoric is described as more nuanced than the market suggests, more a regulatory reset than ideological rejection of data centers. The author thinks actual spending could surprise positively versus what is now discounted.
Risk: de-grossing remains acute. Nasdaq has broken its 200-day moving average while the S&P sits just above it, which needs to hold. Negative gamma leaves scope for violent moves in either direction.

The author's gut view is that fundamental uncertainty justifies the de-rating, but the last leg has overextended in some assets as forced de-risking entrenched. Higher quality tech such as TSMC and ASML is named.
What changes the narrative: political reflexivity around AI investment and growth, stabilization in funding markets, and evidence that spending and demand remain intact.

The author stands by the pre-election view. The S&P has been higher 12 months after each of the 19 midterms since 1950, a 12-month observation and not a one-month forecast. Expects defensive positioning into the weekend, but says such episodes have historically been buying opportunities.

tension_points.bull_case: Like 1998, the shock is about liquidity and forced de-grossing while the AI growth engine stays intact. Leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets, and delayed data centers do not destroy compute demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Like 2000, the scale of spending and uncertainty about returns could mean the buildout economics are wrong and this is the start of a structural technology unwind.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Demand, utilization and returns failing to hold, and the S&P failing to hold its 200-day moving average.

theme_stances.key_argument: The author leans toward a 1998-style liquidity crisis and buying opportunity over a 2000-style structural unwind.
The market has latched onto power and permitting, arguably the least important of four concerns, and constrained supply is not disappearing demand.
